title: Renovate

story: Every Saturday at 03:17 UTC, a workflow in fcp wakes up and updates dependencies. It opens one pull request per app: the client, the cloud backend, the MCP server, connect-api, the frontend and the SDK, plus one more for the gRPC packages. On Monday morning up to seven dependency PRs are waiting for people. Some are red, and nothing stops one of them from carrying a version that was published the night before.

The workflow that does this is 362 lines of shell and YAML that only fcp has, and only fcp's people can fix. Meanwhile the pinned action hashes and the Docker base images, which this workflow never touches, get older every week.
hook.question: How do we keep every kind of dependency up to date with fewer, calmer PRs, without maintaining our own update bot?

p: Renovate is an open-source bot that does this job for many ecosystems at once. Three parts are involved. Managers are Renovate's readers, one per kind of file: npm reads package.json, pep621 reads Python's pyproject.toml, dockerfile reads FROM lines, and github-actions reads the uses: lines of workflows, including the pinned hashes and their version comments from the pinning lesson. The configuration, a renovate.json5 file at the repo root, says which updates to offer, when, grouped how, and reviewed by whom. And the run is Renovate itself, which reads the repo, looks up newer versions in each registry, and opens or updates one PR per branch it decides on.

Renovate also keeps its own PRs healthy: on every run it rebases them on the latest main, so a PR from the 1st of the month is still mergeable on the 10th. Everything that the weekly workflow does in shell becomes a few lines of configuration that the whole Renovate community maintains.

read.h: The pace: a monthly schedule and a waiting period
p: Two settings change Monday morning the most. schedule says when Renovate may open new PRs; here only between 2 and 6 in the morning on the 1st of each month, in Israel's time zone. A few larger PRs get better reviews than many small ones arriving all month. minimumReleaseAge says how old a release must be before Renovate offers it; here 7 days. Most broken releases are fixed or removed from the registry within days, and a package hijacked to steal secrets, like the GitHub Action in the pinning lesson, is usually caught within days too. With internalChecksFilter set to strict, Renovate does not even create a branch for a version that is too young.

rangeStrategy: update-lockfile keeps the ranges in package.json as they are and only moves the lockfile, the way npm update does, which is what the weekly workflow does today. JSON5 is JSON that allows comments and unquoted keys, so the file can explain itself.

code.text:
{
  $schema: "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  extends: ["config:recommended"],
  timezone: "Asia/Jerusalem",
  schedule: ["* 2-6 1 * *"],               // new PRs only on the 1st of the month
  minimumReleaseAge: "7 days",
  internalChecksFilter: "strict",          // no branch at all until the release is 7 days old
  rangeStrategy: "update-lockfile",        // like npm update: stay inside our version ranges
  lockFileMaintenance: { enabled: true },  // a monthly refresh of indirect dependencies
  prConcurrentLimit: 10,
  enabledManagers: ["npm", "pep621", "pip-compile", "dockerfile", "github-actions"],
  ignorePaths: ["**/node_modules/**", "ohif/**"],

notes.text: Renovate's base preset: sensible defaults, such as separate PRs for major versions.
Five cron fields: any minute, hours 2 to 6, day 1, every month, any weekday. Renovate still runs daily to rebase.
A version younger than this is not offered. The lab shows Renovate holding back versions that are too young.
The managers fcp needs. Renovate knows dozens more, from Terraform to Helm.
Folders Renovate must not touch, such as vendored code.

p: A packageRule matches some updates, by folder, manager, package name or update type, and changes how they are handled. groupName puts everything that matches into one PR with one branch, and reviewers asks the right team to review it. So the frontend's npm updates arrive as one PR for the frontend guild, as today, but once a month instead of every week.

Rules apply in order, and a later rule wins over an earlier one for the same update. That is how the major rule works: groupName: null removes major updates from their group, so each major version arrives as its own PR that can be reviewed, or repaired, alone. The gRPC rule comes after it on purpose, because the gRPC packages must move together in the client and the cloud, majors included.

code.text:
packageRules: [
  { matchFileNames: ["frontend/**"], groupName: "frontend npm", reviewers: ["team:frontend-guild"] },
  { matchFileNames: ["cloud/rhinoCloud/**"], groupName: "cloud python", reviewers: ["team:backend-guild"] },
  { matchFileNames: ["client/**"], groupName: "client python", reviewers: ["team:backend-guild"] },
  { matchUpdateTypes: ["major"], groupName: null },   // one PR per major, so it can be fixed alone
  { matchPackageNames: ["grpcio", "grpcio-tools", "grpcio-status", "grpcio-health-checking", "protobuf"],
    groupName: "grpc stack", reviewers: ["team:backend-guild"] },   // client + cloud move together, majors too
  { matchManagers: ["github-actions"], groupName: "github actions" },
  { matchManagers: ["dockerfile"], groupName: "base images" },
  { matchPackageNames: ["RhinoHealth/byte"], enabled: false },     // Byte's own script moves this pin
],

notes.text: Every npm update under frontend/ lands in one PR, reviewed by the frontend guild team.
Majors leave their group here. Order matters: the rules below can still put some of them back in a group.
Matched by package name in every folder, so the client and the cloud get the same gRPC version in one PR.
Pinned action hashes and their version comments are updated together.
enabled: false turns updates off for one package; Byte's maintainers move that pin with their own script.

p: Renovate exists as a hosted GitHub App, but fcp needs a feature it does not allow: postUpgradeTasks, commands that run on the branch after an update, such as regenerating a requirements file. So we run Renovate ourselves, in a small workflow on fcp-runner-set, every night. The nightly run only rebases and refreshes; new PRs still appear only on the 1st, because of the schedule in the config.

Look at where the token comes from. A PR that a workflow opens with its own GITHUB_TOKEN does not start other workflows, so Renovate's PRs would get no CI at all. The workflow therefore mints a token from a small GitHub App made for opening PRs, the same App the weekly workflow uses today. Commands are a second wall: Renovate runs a post-upgrade command only if it appears, letter for letter, in the allowed list.

code.text:
name: Renovate
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '41 1 * * *'   # daily, so open PRs stay rebased; new PRs still only on the 1st
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  renovate:
    runs-on: fcp-runner-set
    steps:
      - id: app-token
        uses: actions/create-github-app-token@bcd2ba49218906704ab6c1aa796996da409d3eb1 # v3.2.0
        with:
          app-id: ${{ secrets.RHINO_PR_CREATOR_APP_ID }}
          private-key: ${{ secrets.RHINO_PR_CREATOR_PRIVATE_KEY }}
      - uses: renovatebot/github-action@f0f41e5f2e706165f6814b1d0f0d0e319de7d1d9 # v46.3.8
        with:
          token: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}
        env:
          RENOVATE_REPOSITORIES: RhinoHealth/fcp
          RENOVATE_ALLOWED_COMMANDS: '["make -C cloud/rhinoCloud update-deps"]'

notes.text: Five cron fields in UTC: 01:41 every day.
The job's own token only reads. Every write uses the App token below.
Mints a one-hour token for the PR-creator App, so Renovate's PRs trigger the normal CI.
Pinned by full SHA, like every action. Renovate will keep this pin up to date too.
Only these exact commands may run after an update; anything else in the config is refused.

deeper.h: Go deeper: what stays, and what fixes the red ones
p: Before the first real run, Renovate is tested twice without side effects: in CI with RENOVATE_DRY_RUN=full, which logs every PR it would open, and on a laptop with the local platform, which you do in the lab. The old weekly workflow is deleted in the same PR, with no fallback.

GitHub's own Dependabot stays, but only for security alerts, with its PR limit at zero, because Renovate opens security fixes at once, outside the monthly schedule. And when a Renovate PR goes red, a routine called an upgrade fixer, the same agent as Nova started by the failed check, tries to repair that one PR, so people mostly see green dependency PRs.

lab.title: Ask Renovate what it would do
needs: Node 24.11 or newer for Renovate (nvm use 24)
The gh CLI, logged in; Renovate uses its token only to read public GitHub tags
About 400 MB of disk; the first npx of Renovate takes a minute
lab.goal: Run Renovate locally on a small repo with old dependencies, read which branches it would open, see the waiting period hold versions back, and regroup the updates with packageRules.

guess.q: The config says minimumReleaseAge: "7 days". vitest released 5.0.3 fifteen days ago and 5.0.5 two days ago. Which version does Renovate offer today?

options.why: 5.0.5 is younger than 7 days, so Renovate holds it back and lists it as pending.

options.text: 5.0.3, the newest version that is at least 7 days old.
options.why: minimumReleaseAge filters out versions that are too young; the newest old-enough version is offered.

options.text: Nothing, until every version is at least 7 days old.
options.why: Renovate does not wait for the whole series; it offers the newest version that passes the age rule.

  }
}
EOF
cat > .github/workflows/ci.yml <<'EOF'
name: CI
on: [pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
EOF
printf 'FROM node:22-bookworm-slim\n' > Dockerfile
cat > renovate.json5 <<'EOF'
{
  $schema: "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  extends: ["config:recommended"],
  timezone: "Asia/Jerusalem",
  schedule: ["* 2-6 1 * *"],     // new PRs only on the 1st of the month
  minimumReleaseAge: "7 days",   // nothing younger than a week
  packageRules: [
    { matchManagers: ["npm"], groupName: "npm" },
  ],
}
EOF
printf 'report.json\n' > .gitignore && git add -A && git commit -qm 'A small repo with old dependencies'

lab.build: Regroup the updates the way fcp will. In renovate.json5, add three packageRules after the npm one: all github-actions updates in a group called "github actions", all dockerfile updates in a group called "base images", and, last, every major update out of its group (groupName: null). Validate, run Renovate again with the same command, and list the branches again.
checks: actions/checkout's patch update is now on the branch renovate/github-actions.
Each major update has a branch of its own, such as renovate/zod-4.x and renovate/vitest-5.x, and renovate/major-npm is gone.
typescript appears twice: the minor update in renovate/npm and the major one alone.
In the Fix it step, the validator names the misspelled option.
lab.fix: A teammate wanted updates 'a bit faster' and edited the config by hand. Change minimumReleaseAge: "7 days" to minimumReleaseAg: "1 day" (a typo and a shorter wait), and run the validator. It fails and names the unknown option, which would otherwise be ignored without a word. Put the correct name back, and decide whether 1 day is a good idea, given what you saw in the tooYoung lists.
explain: What does a manager do, and which managers found something in your scratch repo?
Why does the major rule come after the group rules, and what changes if you move it first?
Why does the Renovate workflow use an App token instead of the job's GITHUB_TOKEN?

check.q: The config has minimumReleaseAge: "7 days". A package published a new version yesterday. What does Renovate do with it today?

options.text: Holds it back as pending until it is 7 days old, and offers an older version if one qualifies
options.why: Young versions are filtered out, so a broken or hijacked release has a week to be noticed before it reaches us.

options.text: Opens the PR now and marks it as draft for 7 days
options.why: With internalChecksFilter strict, Renovate does not even create a branch for a version that is too young.

options.text: Ignores the package until next month
options.why: The age rule is about versions, not packages. Older versions of the same package can still be offered.

check.q: packageRules has a group rule for frontend/** and, after it, { matchUpdateTypes: ["major"], groupName: null }. A major update of React arrives in frontend/. Where does it go?

options.text: Into the frontend npm group, because that rule matched first
options.why: Every matching rule applies in order, and a later rule overrides an earlier one.

options.text: Into a PR of its own, because the later major rule removes the group
options.why: groupName: null from the later rule wins, so each major can be reviewed and repaired alone.

options.text: Nowhere: majors are disabled by groupName: null
options.why: groupName: null only removes the grouping. enabled: false is what turns updates off.

check.q: Why does the self-hosted Renovate workflow mint an App token instead of using the job's GITHUB_TOKEN?

options.why: Registries are read with their own access, not with GitHub's token. That is not the reason.

options.text: GITHUB_TOKEN expires too quickly for Renovate
options.why: It lasts as long as the job, which is enough for one Renovate run.

options.text: PRs and pushes made with GITHUB_TOKEN do not start other workflows, so Renovate's PRs would get no CI
options.why: GitHub blocks that to prevent loops. An App token's PRs start CI like anyone else's.

p: fcp replaces its weekly dependency workflow with a self-hosted Renovate: grouped PRs by app with today's reviewers, new PRs only on the 1st, nothing younger than 7 days, majors alone, the gRPC stack together, and pinned actions and base images included. The same pattern then covers the infrastructure and gitops repos for Terraform providers, Helm charts and actions.

Renovate stays a plain bot. When one of its PRs goes red, an upgrade fixer, a routine that reacts to a failed check on a renovate/ branch, tries to repair that one PR, so people see few dependency PRs, and green ones.

tickets.why: renovate.json5 for fcp, the self-hosted workflow, the dry run, and deleting the weekly workflow.
Renovate for the infrastructure and gitops repos: providers, charts and actions.
The routine trigger watches failed checks on renovate/* branches, which only exist once Renovate runs.
The frontend upgrade fixer repairs one failed npm Renovate PR at a time.

words.plain: An open-source bot that finds newer versions of your dependencies and opens PRs for them, driven by a config file.
Renovate's reader for one kind of file, such as npm for package.json or github-actions for workflow files.
A rule that matches some updates and changes how they are handled, such as their group or reviewers.
Updates that share a groupName and therefore arrive together in one branch and one PR.
How old a version must be before Renovate offers it; younger versions wait as pending.
Commands Renovate runs on the branch after an update; only commands on the allowed list can run.

review.q: Write the two settings that make Renovate open PRs only on the 1st of the month and skip versions younger than a week.
review.a: schedule: ["* 2-6 1 * *"] (with a timezone) and minimumReleaseAge: "7 days", plus internalChecksFilter: "strict" so no branch is created early.

review.q: How do you make every major update arrive as its own PR, while minor updates stay grouped?
review.a: Put { matchUpdateTypes: ["major"], groupName: null } after the group rules. Rules apply in order, so the later one removes the group for majors only.

review.q: Name the two walls in the self-hosted Renovate workflow.
review.a: The job's own token is read-only and writes use a short App token from the PR-creator App, and post-upgrade commands run only if they are on RENOVATE_ALLOWED_COMMANDS.

remember: Renovate turns dependency updates into configuration: managers find them, packageRules group them, and a monthly schedule with a 7-day wait keeps them few and calm.
